A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VSF research and contain readable main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Matching methods, benchmark results, and figures support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-generation evaluations, hyperparameter sweeps, component ablations, runtime measurements, and qualitative Wan video results.

after.justification: V4 retains original experiments and adds human validation, Flux results, trained evaluator benchmarks, sensitivity analyses, and artistic-generation experiments.

M1.justification: The core sign-flip attention, masking, duplication, and padding removal remain. V4 adds negative-embedding extrapolation for Flux Schnell using a mean-padding reference and scale 8 (Appendix G), following v1's unsuccessful Flux application. It also introduces QLoRA-trained NegAwareQwen-7B/32B evaluation models (Appendix O).

E1.justification: The existing 200-prompt component-removal benchmark is retained and named NegGenBench. V4 expands evaluated tasks to style avoidance and abstract/unconventional-aesthetic generation (Appendices M–N), and adds supervised negation/quality judging on a newly annotated image collection (Appendix O).

E2.justification: V4 adds Nano Banana to the external generation comparison and introduces evaluator comparisons against LLaMA Maverick and Qwen-2.5-VL-32B, each with and without chain-of-thought prompting (Table 7). The Wan qualitative comparison drops NAG, retaining only original generation versus VSF. The main image comparators remain, with NAG++ renamed NAG Strong.

E3.justification: V4 adds a VSF Quality setting, human scoring of four methods on ten prompts with two seeds, and a prompt-level 90/10 split with three-level annotations for evaluator training/testing. Table 7 binarizes partial adherence, whereas Table 8 retains fractional scores. Wan qualitative evaluation changes from 1.3B to 14B; the runtime experiment still uses 1.3B.

E4.justification: V4 adds quantitative alpha/beta sensitivity on 30 prompts (Figure 19), human–MLLM agreement and quality-score analyses (Table 4/Figure 9), CLIP negation diagnostics, and new failure cases. The original trade-off and component-ablation curves remain unchanged in Figure 6. Image and Wan case studies are substantially replaced.

E5.justification: V1's McNemar-test description and Table 2 p<10^-6 annotations disappear. V4 adds linear/logarithmic regression fits and R-squared reporting for human–MLLM quality agreement (Figure 9). The main benchmark still uses two seeds, without newly reported confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Existing Table 2 scores remain unchanged after renaming. V4 adds VSF Quality scores of 0.980/0.420/0.986 and Nano Banana scores of 0.985/0.498/0.980 for positive/negative/quality metrics. It also adds Flux, human-validation, evaluator-benchmark, and rescoring results (Tables 3–8), and replaces qualitative examples. These additions do not establish improvements under unchanged settings.

T1.justification: V4 introduces explicit attention-derived token weights and weighted-subtraction equations (6–8), followed by Appendix B's algebraic equivalence proof. V1 only asserted that equivalence after Equation 6. This is a limited formal addition concerning an already-stated identity.

C1.justification: V4 expands the stated contributions to include NegGenBench and trained negation-aware evaluators. Its abstract now claims effective Flux Schnell integration, and its conclusion adds creative, abstract, and unconventional-aesthetic applications. The central claim of stronger negative adherence with low computational overhead remains.

C2.justification: V4 explains why near-ceiling MLLM quality scores poorly distinguish quality, supported by human comparisons (Appendix F). It adds evaluator insensitivity as an explanation for unchanged bias-ablation results and interprets artistic generation as countering preference-induced style homogenization. Failure discussions change substantially, including removal of v1's conclusion that Wan VSF and NAG outputs are overall comparable.

D1.justification: V4 adds VSF pseudocode, explicit VSF preset hyperparameters, Flux embedding-processing instructions, and QLoRA training and annotation/splitting details. It first specifies 28 steps for the retained CFG baseline. Conversely, v1's available-code/ComfyUI statement and link are replaced by promises to release code, data, and models after publication.

R1.justification: Positioning expands into trained negation evaluators, machine unlearning, and aesthetic/preference alignment, citing Qwen2.5-VL, QLoRA, Gandikota et al., VisionReward, LAPIS, and human-values literature. The core CFG/NASA/NAG/Dynamic Negative Guidance lineage remains. V1's separate Feedback Guidance citation is removed.

P1.justification: V4 extensively reorganizes the narrative into separate experiments, results, and discussion sections, moving substantial background, implementation, evaluation, and qualitative material into appendices A–S with a contents list. Method explanations and results prose are substantially rewritten, and reproducibility and LLM-use statements are added.

P2.justification: V4 combines the existing trade-off and component-ablation plots into Figure 6 and relocates the hyperparameter grid and quality examples. It replaces image/video montages, removes the WEF gallery, and adds style, failure, agreement, and sensitivity figures plus several evaluation tables. Table 1 gains open-/closed-weight groupings and metric-direction indicators.

improvement.justification: V1 acknowledged unreliable MLLM scoring but only mentioned human comparison without reporting its results. V4 supplies human validation and judge-agreement analysis (Tables 3–4/Figure 9), benchmarks a trained negation evaluator, and provides additional generator ratings (Tables 7–8). This substantially strengthens validation of the central negative-guidance finding. The small human sample, removed significance reporting, deferred code-release statement, and Table 8 positive scores that contradict claimed reuse from Table 2 remain meaningful drawbacks, but the stronger validation provides a substantial net gain.
